items.title: Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio: Quantifying the Dual-Track Mechanism of Gender Assignment in Latvian Loanwords
items.content: arXiv:2609.03930v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing research has repeatedly observed the tendency for English loanwords to cluster in the masculine gender across different recipient languages, yet the origin of this pattern remains difficult to determine, as fixed morphological rules and default assignments are frequently analysed together. This study proposes the Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio (FSDR) to quantify the degree of reliance on fixed derivational suffixes across different genders, and to distinguish between morphological anchoring and free-choice in distribution. By examining 1,832 Latvian noun lemma types, the results reveal a significant FSDR asymmetry within the loanword system: feminine loanwords rely significantly more on fixed derivational suffixes, while masculine loanwords are more concentrated in the free-choice zone. This pattern exhibits loanword specificity and has become more pronounced in contemporary usage. FSDR therefore provides a quantitative framework for testing default gender and shows how masculine default can be activated and reinforced under language contact.
items.author: Yelingyun Zhang, Atis Kapenieks, Marina Platonova
items.summary: This study introduces the Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio to analyze morphological gender assignment mechanisms for English loanwords integrated into Latvian. The quantitative analysis demonstrates that feminine loanword assignment relies strictly on fixed derivational suffixes, whereas masculine assignments follow default lexical pathways. This work offers a formal quantitative metric for morphosyntactic borrowing in linguistic typology.
items.reasoning: A specialized linguistic morphology study with sound methodology within linguistics, but narrow implications for mainstream AI and NLP practitioners.

items.title: A hybrid pipeline for dynamic ontology-based semantic mapping
items.content: arXiv:2609.03891v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Semantic mapping plays a crucial role in the ability of a robot to interact with objects, operate and navigate a complex environment. The most common pipeline for semantic mapping consists of geometric mapping and localization (SLAM), perception, semantic fusion and semantic representation. However, more recent works also integrate a form of prior knowledge in their application, most notably knowledge graphs or semantic scene graphs, to improve contextual understanding of the environment. In this paper, we present a hybrid pipeline for semantic mapping. Our system incorporates an external calibrated camera using homography projection for geometric mapping and localization, combined with object detection, persistent object tracking and ontology driven semantic updates to build a dynamic semantic world model. Linear regression models are also used for correction of the estimated values of real world coordinates. The system continuously updates object instances, spatial properties and semantic relations based on real time sensory data. Ontologies are selected as form of knowledge representation due to their hierarchical structure, semantic expressiveness and support for dynamic world modelling.
items.author: Konstantinos Dimitropoulos, Ioannis Hatzilygeroudis
items.summary: This paper presents a hybrid robotic semantic mapping pipeline that merges external homography-based camera localization with persistent object tracking and formal ontologies. By incorporating ontological priors, the framework enhances contextual scene understanding and dynamic spatial reasoning beyond standard geometric SLAM. This contributes to more structured, queryable spatial memory for indoor service robotics.

items.title: Comparing Retrieval Methods for Academic Advisor Discovery: A Six-Method Study of 768 CS Faculty Profiles Across 9 US Universities
items.content: arXiv:2609.03901v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present a comparative evaluation of six information retrieval methods for the task of academic advisor discovery: ranking CS faculty members by relevance to a graduate applicant's research interest statement. The methods span sparse lexical matching (Jaccard overlap, TF-IDF, BM25), dense semantic retrieval (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings), hybrid score fusion, and learning-to-rank. Evaluation uses a new domain-specific collection: 768 faculty profiles scraped from 9 US CS departments, with 162 graded relevance judgments (grade 0/1/2) across 5 queries representing distinct graduate student research profiles. Across all five queries, Reranked achieves the highest mean NDCG@10 (0.477, std 0.138), followed by Semantic (0.450), Hybrid (0.421), BM25 (0.406), Jaccard (0.303), and TF-IDF (0.246). After Bonferroni correction across all 15 pairwise comparisons, TF-IDF is significantly worse than BM25, Semantic, Hybrid, and Reranked; no other pairwise difference survives correction at 5 queries. A field ablation reveals that biography alone (NDCG 0.634) outperforms the full model combining biography with research area tags (0.593). A controlled experiment shows that concatenating arXiv paper abstracts reduces NDCG@10 by 0.176, motivating a late-fusion architecture. All code, scrapers, and relevance labels are released openly.

The paper releases a specialized domain benchmark for academic advisor matching.

items.title: Equilibria for Networks of Linear Translational Springs
items.content: arXiv:2609.03143v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We use tools from nonlinear algebra to study the equilibria of small linear translational spring networks. Specifically we use the techniques of homotopy continuation, monodromy, and parameter homotopy (a.k.a. cheater homotopy) to solve all rigid linear translational spring networks up to $5$ nodes in both $2$ and $3$ dimensions. We describe a method of implementing parameter homotopy that arises naturally from the physical structure of the system. We give precise total degree bounds on the maximum number of solutions for general planar spring networks. We discuss further efficiency gains obtained from polyhedral homotopy methods. We compare the computation efficiency of these techniques against a baseline of Newton's method.
items.author: Luke Oeding, Ethan Clayton, Jackson Elsea, Nicholas Wang, Adam Rutkowski
items.summary: This study applies nonlinear computational algebra, including homotopy continuation and parameter homotopy, to compute all mechanical equilibrium states for rigid linear translational spring networks up to five nodes. The authors establish explicit degree bounds on total equilibrium solutions in 2D and 3D while highlighting significant computational advantages over standard Newton solvers. The findings advance theoretical kinematics for multistable elastic mechanisms.
items.reasoning: Rigorous applied algebraic geometry solving a foundational mechanics problem, though primarily of interest to theoretical kinematics researchers.

items.title: A Therapist for People Who Think the World Might End: An Interview with Daystar Eld (Damon Sasi)
items.content:
I sat down with therapist and writer Damon Sasi, better known online as Daystar Eld, for one of the conversations I’ve found myself referencing most often since recording it.

We talk about what’s bullshit and what isn’t in therapy, therapy for rationalists, and how to stay psychologically healthy when you genuinely believe the end of the world may be coming.

We also cover executive function, whether therapists are sometimes substitutes for friendships, and what actually helps people change. We talk about rationality and effective altruism, dating, and the modern dating crisis.

We spend a lot of time on AI companions, AI girlfriends and boyfriends, wireheading, chatbot psychosis, and what happens when artificial partners can be tailored to us more perfectly than another human being ever could.

And of course we discuss rationalist fiction, Pokémon, the influence of Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality, and his magnum opus: Pokémon: The Origin of Species!

items.title: A Non-Formulable Theorem: A Fundamental Limit of Finite Syntactic Systems and Its Consequences for Security and AI
items.content: arXiv:2609.04086v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: For every coherent and sufficiently expressive finite syntactic system S, we prove the existence of at least one theorem that S cannot produce autonomously. The result is a metatheorem: it proves the existence of a theorem, and applies to every finite syntactic system - security mechanisms, AI systems, formal verifiers, legal systems, economic models, and the formal system in which it is itself proved.
items.author: Fabio F. G. Buono
items.summary: This theoretical note formulates a metatheorem demonstrating that every coherent and sufficiently expressive finite syntactic system contains at least one theorem it cannot autonomously produce. The paper discusses implications for automated formal verification, legal systems, and foundational AI limits. It contributes a philosophical and formal analysis of inherent completeness boundaries in computational systems.

items.title: Evaluating GNNs for Success Prediction in Artist Collaboration Networks
items.content: arXiv:2609.02920v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: As the music industry becomes an increasingly collaborative effort, understanding the underlying structures of the artist network has become a focal point in cultural data analytics. This study expands on the previous analyses of the Italian and Danish networks by introducing a novel dataset of the Polish music scene. By utilizing methodologies used in the prior studies, this work enables a direct comparison between three distinct European music landscapes and allows to merged the created networks into one. Furthermore, this research introduces a framework to test the efficacy of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for artist popularity predictions based on the metadata and the position in the network. The statistical analysis revealed that the Polish and tri-national network exhibit similar properties and clustering behaviours, consistent with prior models. An evaluation of the predictive architectures reveals that while GNN models achieve a comparable F1-macro scores to the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) in specific cases however the MLP remains a superior model regarding the success metric. The results suggest that internal node features - such as genre and label affiliation might carry more predictive capabilities than the topology of the network. The higher performance of the GNN models in the tri-national network might also suggests that the relational features become more informative when the network spans multiple linguistic and geographic boundaries, with the GNNs potentially capturing complex 'bridge' structures between the merged networks.

items.content_html: arXiv:2609.02920v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the music industry becomes an increasingly collaborative effort, understanding the underlying structures of the artist network has become a focal point in cultural data analytics. This study expands on the previous analyses of the Italian and Danish networks by introducing a novel dataset of the Polish music scene. By utilizing methodologies used in the prior studies, this work enables a direct comparison between three distinct European music landscapes and allows to merged the created networks into one. Furthermore, this research introduces a framework to test the efficacy of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for artist popularity predictions based on the metadata and the position in the network. The statistical analysis revealed that the Polish and tri-national network exhibit similar properties and clustering behaviours, consistent with prior models. An evaluation of the predictive architectures reveals that while GNN models achieve a comparable F1-macro scores to the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) in specific cases however the MLP remains a superior model regarding the success metric. The results suggest that internal node features - such as genre and label affiliation might carry more predictive capabilities than the topology of the network. The higher performance of the GNN models in the tri-national network might also suggests that the relational features become more informative when the network spans multiple linguistic and geographic boundaries, with the GNNs potentially capturing complex 'bridge' structures between the merged networks.

items.title: Opening mind by opening architecture: analysis strategies
items.content: arXiv:2609.03719v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In numerical signal processing for electroacoustic composition, the progressive loss of specific development and research environments caused by the increasing use of digital market tools has favoured the dominance of the closed-architecture audio processor model. This model, while powerful, envisions the possibility of describing output data about its perceived characteristics, but at the cost of ignoring its internal process and interacting systems, which become complex, powerful environments but closed in an inscrutable black box, a loss we must consider. Any digital signal processing technique tells a story. Just as the words of a language incorporate social, historical and technical polysemic layers, a signal processor has its own story of implementation, a gradual technological achievement with its inevitable aesthetic consequences. Through the looking-glass of literature, one can access those environments with renewed awareness by reestablishing a scientific method and an attitude to research. In this specific case, starting from the case study of Manfred Schroeder's historical reverbs, we illustrate the process of building analytical evaluation tools, as well as practical implementation, at the basis of a conscious study path.

items.title: Concept of a Sensor Test Environment for Dusty Agricultural Conditions
items.content: arXiv:2609.03895v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dust in agriculture presents a significant challenge for autonomous agricultural machinery. Dust can impair the performance of sensors and algorithms. This work, therefore, presents a concept for a proving ground consisting of an indoor and outdoor area. The indoor area comprises a laboratory test bench where dust circulates in a closed system and a test hall where life-size objects can be placed. The outdoor area features dedicated test setups that enable reproducible data to be recorded with and without dust during real-world agriculture work. The proving ground and the setups are visualized in 3D.

items.summary: The paper outlines a testing environment design consisting of indoor closed-loop dust circulation chambers and outdoor agricultural fields to benchmark autonomous sensors under heavy dust. It details proving ground configurations to evaluate perception hardware degradation under field conditions.

items.title: Automated Weld Seam Recognition and 3D Mapping for Robotic Post Processing Using Photogrammetry and Semantic Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2609.03970v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate identification of weld seam geometries is essential for automated robotic post processing operations such as grinding, finishing, and inspection. For large workpieces, complete surface scanning using high precision laser scanners or structured light sensors can be time consuming and often generates substantial amount of data that are not relevant. This paper presents an experimental vision based pipeline for the approximate localization of weld seams. This serves as a preliminary stage before high precision measurement. The proposed approach aims to reduce the overall scanning effort and data acquisition efficiency. The proposed method includes capturing images of the workpiece from multiple viewpoints, identifying weld seams from the images using semantic segmentation, reconstructing the workpiece using photogrammetry, and projection of identified weld seams into the reconstructed model.
items.author: Augustin Raju, Abilash Madavath, Chandra Yuvesh Aubeeluck, Nicolas Pyschny, Felix Hackel\"oer, Florian Zwanzig
items.summary: This work introduces a vision-based pipeline that combines multi-view photogrammetry with semantic segmentation for automated weld seam detection and 3D mapping on large industrial structures. Designed as an efficient preliminary localization step, it filters irrelevant geometry before deploying high-precision surface scanners. This significantly reduces data capture volume and scanning latency in robotic manufacturing post-processing.

items.title: Personal Effort to Reduce Biorisk
items.content:
I'm
pretty worried
about how AI might change the world a lot very soon.  In some of these
cases things go very wrong very quickly, in others things go very
right very quickly, but I'm increasingly (relative to

2024)
expecting a messy middle path where, whether we end up with a good or
bad outcome, things might get weird for a while.  Our supply chains
are fragile, fulfilment is largely just-in-time, and if we'll suddenly
need way more of some things they might not be available. Thinking a
lot about biosecurity for my day job, I'm especially worried about how
people, AIs, or some combination might release something to spread
through the population.

What can we do about this?  A few months ago Chris Bakerlee (program
officer on Coefficient Giving's biosecurity
and pandemic preparedness team) wrote up 10
big projects for reducing bio x-risk.  Working on any of these
professionally would be really valuable.  Looking over the list,
however, it occurred
to me that most of them have solid actions we can do at the
individual level.

Several of these have the form "X is important, figure out how to get
countries to have X in an emergency", and since you likely care about
your own welfare much more than that of strangers, they're typically
worth just going and doing.  Not on altruistic grounds, but they're
competitive with other ways to spend your money to improve your
own life in expectation.  And this is the opposite of hoarding during
a disaster: buying in advance stimulates pre-disaster production while
also reducing disaster-time pressure.

Walking through the list:

- "Boost countries' food stockpiles by >25%, especially
countries with high industrial capacity": store food.  If you
have some space and like to cook, maintaining a deep pantry with three
months of food foregoes ~$9/year/person in investment returns....

items.title: OBER+: Continuity-Aware Reporting and Traceable Continuous Improvement in Outcome-Based Education
items.content: arXiv:2609.03770v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Institutions practising outcome-based education compute learning outcome attainment routinely, while reviews of curriculum analytics report an absence of evidence on how that computation informs decisions. This paper presents OBER+, an extension of a deployed institutional attainment platform that computes the step from a measured shortfall to an evaluated corrective action. Five connected stages accumulate attainment across deliveries of a course, signal a shortfall and a persistent shortfall, grade it on cutoffs the regulator already uses, record the decision against a catalogue of practices annotated with their evidence, log the change, and quantify the subsequent movement in the shortfall. A further rule compares successive statements of an outcome, so attainment is never read as a series across a point at which the outcome changed. Applying the rules to the live record of two real courses produced three results. Every outcome of a core course was substantively redefined between consecutive deliveries, with subject matter moving between outcome numbers, so a naive reading would have reported a twenty-five point collapse between quantities that do not refer to the same learning. Recomputing the platform's figures from its documented rule showed six of ten differing by more than rounding explains, in a pattern that identified a defect since reported to the institution. Across fifteen statement pairs from three transitions, five were identical character for character, and among the ten that were not, the outcome carrying a given number was nearest to a differently numbered earlier outcome in six, a result resting on an ordering of similarities and requiring no threshold and no labelling. The contribution is a computational design for outcome-based reporting, stated as rules any attainment platform can implement, with evidence of what they make visible in a live institutional record.

items.summary: This paper presents OBER+, an educational analytics platform designed to link student learning outcome shortfalls directly to evaluated corrective actions. It provides an institutional auditing tool for outcome-based educational administration.

items.title: Corner Cases: Headland Coverage Path Planning for Autonomous Driving in Arable Farming
items.content: arXiv:2609.04103v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents a new method for headland coverage path planning for arable fields. Several earlier approaches suggest covering the headland with nested polygons and smooth turns, however, covering the field corners entirely requires manoeuvres with reversing. In the new method, the polygon corners are modified to allow a reversing turn. A comparison to two other methods considering gap, overlap, and crossing the field boundary shows an improvement in the coverage result especially in field corners of around 90 degrees, and 240 degrees and above. Applicability of the new method is shown with several examples of real polygonal field maps.
items.author: Riikka Soitinaho, Timo Oksanen
items.summary: The authors present a headland coverage path planning method for autonomous agricultural tractors that incorporates reversing maneuvers to completely cover sharp field corners. Benchmarks across irregular polygonal field maps demonstrate improved boundary adherence and reduced coverage gaps compared to conventional smoothing techniques. This work optimizes operational coverage efficiency in precision farming.
items.reasoning: A specialized kinematic path-planning solution for agricultural automation with clear practical utility but narrow domain focus.

items.title: Building a High Talent Density Organization
items.content:
I wrote this for the SaferAI team. I'm publishing it with some small edits, in case it's useful to other orgs. A note on scope, this post is about sourcing candidates specifically. It doesn't cover how we define a role before opening it, how we assess candidates once they're in the process,....

I recently listened to this podcast with Adam Ward, who runs talent at Cursor, and read this post by Sam Altman on hiring. These two resources prompted me to rethink how we approach talent building. Below are some recommendations inspired by them, and a few taken directly from them.

High talent density should be one of our top priorities. The way we currently think about hiring is: draft a job ad, publish it, advertise it a little, passively wait for the funnel to fill, then run the funnel and aim to pick the best person out of everyone who applied.

Doing it this way, it's unlikely that we’ll get the best possible candidates for the role, as they probably won’t be applying in the first place. We need to actively look for the best people, and convince them that SaferAI is a great place for them to be. Some pointers to achieve this: 

## Actively Source the Best People

- Go through our employees' networks. Ask them directly, and try tools that make this easier.
- Leverage the talent building ecosystem. We're lucky that this ecosystem is very rich in AI safety, so let's use it fully. Ask MATS, Constellation, the Anthropic fellowship, Successif, 80,000 Hours and others for shortlists.
- Ask well-connected people for recommendations. It works much better to ask on a call, or over coffee. In an email, people don't take the time to pause and think of names.
- When you ask, ask about a specific skill instead of general excellence. "Who is the best risk modeling researcher you know?" is too vague. "Among the risk modeling researchers you've worked with, who is best at identifying the most strategic questions and building a research agenda around them?" gets better names....

items.title: Satisfying Curiosity Isn't the Same as Understanding
items.content:
If I’m confused or curious about something, I take that to mean I don’t understand it.

This should work in reverse: when an answer to a question satisfies my curiosity, or stops me wondering, does that mean I understand?

Not necessarily.

The example that comes to mind is seemingly overnight going from never hearing of Gracie Abrams, to literally Spotify overriding my play queue to force me to listen to her. [1]So now I was curious – how did, overnight, she become so ubiquitous?

It wasn’t long before I saw her name next to the term “Nepobaby”.

Ah, it's because she's a Nepobaby! Her father is a famous TV producer and film director who, I assume, threw money at her career. Mystery solved. That explains everything, doesn’t it?

No, that was a Fake Explanation, a "because" that doesn't actually hold any anticipatory beliefs. "...because, Nepobaby" is functionally the same as saying"because, magic!"

It doesn’t explain, causally, anything about how that money was deployed, or how she was marketed. It doesn’t elucidate what strategies and tactics were used by her P.R., Management, and Label to get so ubiquitous. It’s also contemptibly elitist[2] and totally discounting the possibility that people genuinely dig her music!

It was a satisfying explanation for me. But it isn’t an explanation at all.

Yes, one slice of humble pie please.

Even the alternative hypothesis I has the air of Fake Explanation. I’m old. [3]She has slowly and steadily been building a following over many years, and what I experienced was simply the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon.

Now I’m worried. I have to do a, kind of, mental model inventory: what are all the other phenomena I feel satisfied about my answers to but are just fake explanations?

Obviously not all of my confidence or satisfaction is due to false explanations, but differentiating is gonna suck....

items.title: Work at Manifund or Mox
items.content:
### What is Manifund?

In What happened to impact markets? Austin laid out a brief history of Manifund and explanation of who and what we are. The perhaps grandiose goal of Manifund is to solve the problem of philanthropic capital allocation. In practice, over a few years, we’ve … done a little bit of that, with some interesting detours?

- We run manifund.org, a platform for funding charitable endeavors. Manifund: runs annual regranting programs offers fiscal sponsorship for grantees handles logistics for programs like ACX Grants and the Falcon Fund
- Right now we’re running Surplus, a startup incubator.
- We also incubated Manifest, now a separate organization.
- And Mox—see below!

Read our Substack to get a sense of what we’re thinking about and what our aims are: right now it’s funding transparency, impact markets, and more.

### What is Mox?

Mox is an incubator and community space in San Francisco. Our vision is to be a space in SF for AI safety, broad-tent EA, and other people doing cool stuff—somewhere people can meet, make connections, work together, learn new things, and feel a sense of community. We:

- offer coworking in San Francisco, for individuals and startup teams
- run events, from weekly clubs and members’ dinners to talks, movie nights, and mixers
- host fellowships like Surplus, Frame, Arbor, and Global Experts Fellowship

Mox was incubated by Manifund and still runs out of the same entity, but is now a substantially separate team and operation.

### Why work at Manifund or Mox?

The biggest reason to work here is excitement about what we’re doing! We want to hire people who are eager to make an impact on the world, whether by creating good communities or getting philanthropic money to the right places....

  • host fellowships like Surplus, Frame, Arbor, and Global Experts Fellowship

Mox was incubated by Manifund and still runs out of the same entity, but is now a substantially separate team and operation.

Why work at Manifund or Mox?

The biggest reason to work here is excitement about what we’re doing! We want to hire people who are eager to make an impact on the world, whether by creating good communities or getting philanthropic money to the right places....

items.title: Biopunk Greenhouse: Trees, Biochar, and Open Plant Biotechnology
items.content:
Spend an afternoon inside Carbocene’s working Oakland greenhouse and garden. We will propagate plants, make biochar, care for a living research collection, and explore how plant biotechnology can be practiced outside the usual boundaries of companies and universities.

​This is a weekly Saturday open greenhouse. Carbocene hosts an informal working session most Saturdays from 3:00–7:00 p.m. for plant propagation, greenhouse care, biochar making, research discussion, and shared experimentation. Each week is listed as a separate Lu.ma event so attendance and occasional schedule changes can be managed individually. Please confirm the date shown on the specific event before attending.

​Future Saturday sessions are open for advance registration. Each week has a separate event page, so please register for the specific date or dates you plan to attend. You are welcome to join once, return regularly, or choose whichever Saturdays fit your schedule.

​Carbocene Industries is an independent nonprofit research organization preserving and advancing biological climate work that might otherwise be lost when funding ends or institutions change direction.

​The greenhouse includes a noncommercial research collection of photosynthesis-enhanced poplar, alongside propagation work, experimental soils, biochar systems, and early research connected to improved photosynthesis, bamboo biotechnology, and durable plant materials.

​This is not a formal lecture or a polished demonstration garden. It is a working research and stewardship site. Each gathering combines teaching, discussion, and practical work based on what the plants and projects need that week.

​No laboratory, gardening, or biotechnology background is required.

### ​What we will do

items.title: ACX Everywhere Fall 26' in Ho Chi Minh city
items.content:
Twice a year, we organize a meetup for people who read LessWrong, Astral Codex Ten, or writers in the broader rationalist sphere in Vietnam. If you're here around mid-September, you're invited to this meetup. Check the link for the precise location and date/time because it may be subject to change if more people RSVP

Location: Around Binh Thanh Dist.

Time & Date: 10 a.m on Saturday, September 12th.

Luma link: https://luma.com/1ig5j0jj
